bmt-2025-power-1-01.title: Answer
bmt-2025-power-1-01.body:
No. A physical model shows that the trefoil cannot be untangled without cutting. A proof is given later by tricolorability (the trefoil is tricolorable, the unknot is not, and tricolorability is unchanged by Reidemeister moves).

**Answer: No**

bmt-2025-power-1-02.title: Answer
bmt-2025-power-1-02.body:
No. The left and right trefoils are mirror images and are different knots: no deformation without cutting turns one into the other (this can be checked with a physical model and proved with finer invariants than those in this round).

**Answer: No**

bmt-2025-power-1-03.title: Systematic case analysis
bmt-2025-power-1-03.body:
Draw the crossing and label its four ends $1,2,3,4$ in order around it. The ends must be joined in pairs by arcs that create no further crossings. Pairing $1$ with $3$ (or $2$ with $4$) would force an arc to cross the strand through the crossing, creating more crossings, so it is not allowed.

The allowed pairings are $\{1,2\},\{3,4\}$ and $\{1,4\},\{2,3\}$ (adjacent ends joined). Each of these (up to the choice of over/under at the crossing, i.e. reflection) gives a diagram of a loop with a single kink, which is undone by one R1 move. Hence every one-crossing diagram represents the unknot. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-1-04.title: Sequence of moves
bmt-2025-power-1-04.body: The left diagram is the right one with a large outer loop wrapped around it, so we pull that loop off. The sequence of Reidemeister moves (as in the official solution) is: two R2 moves, then four R3 moves followed by two R2 moves, and finally one R1 move. At each stage the big outer strand is slid over or under the strands it crosses: R2 moves delete pairs of crossings, R3 moves slide the strand across the remaining crossings, and the last R1 move removes the final kink, leaving the three-crossing diagram on the right. Since only Reidemeister moves were used, the two diagrams are the same knot. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-1-05.title: Sequence of moves
bmt-2025-power-1-05.body: Work from the big outer loop inward. The official sequence is: R2 three times; R3 twice; R3 three times and R2 once; R2 twice and R1 twice; then R2, R2 and finally R1 once. In each stage a highlighted strand is slid across the part of the diagram it overlaps, so that pairs of crossings cancel (R2), strands slide across crossings (R3), and the last kinks are removed (R1), until the circle with no crossings remains. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-1-06a.title: Strategy
bmt-2025-power-1-06a.body:
The unknotter always wins on $T_1$. Call the two crossings on the right the clasp. If the clasp is not resolved alternately, the knot is the unknot, so whoever finishes the clasp can force a win for the unknotter.

Player 1 (the unknotter) first plays the crossing on the left side. Then Player 2 must start the clasp (their only remaining crossings), and Player 1 finishes it non-alternately, giving the unknot.

**Answer: Player 1**

bmt-2025-power-1-06b.title: Strategy
bmt-2025-power-1-06b.body:
Again the unknotter (now Player 2) wins. If Player 1 starts the clasp, Player 2 finishes it non-alternately and the knot is trivial. So Player 1 must play the left crossing first. Then Player 2 resolves the inner clasp crossing opposite to the crossing Player 1 chose; whatever Player 1 does with the last crossing, the result is the unknot (the inner string can be pulled out to remove both inner crossings).

Alternatively: only two of the eight resolutions give a nontrivial knot ($T_1$ and its mirror image), and after any first move the unknotter can always avoid completing either.

**Answer: Player 2**

bmt-2025-power-1-07.title: Strategy by induction on $n$
bmt-2025-power-1-07.body:
Let the clasp be the two crossings at the right; whoever completes the clasp non-alternately (as an unknotter) or wins by finishing it appropriately controls the outcome; in particular if the unknotter finishes the clasp they can force the unknot.

**$n$ even: Player 2 wins.** Base case $T_2$. If Player 1 wants a nontrivial knot: if Player 1 plays on the clasp, Player 2 finishes the clasp and forces the unknot; if Player 1 plays on the left, Player 2 keeps playing on the left until Player 1 must open the clasp, and then finishes it. If Player 1 wants the unknot: Player 2 answers each clasp move with the opposite type on the clasp and each left move with the same type at the other left crossing, so the pairs cancel into an alternating $T_2$, which is nontrivial.

Induction step $T_n\to T_{n-2}$: if Player 1's first move is on the left, Player 2 answers with the opposite resolution at an adjacent left crossing, which unwinds (R2) to a board $T_{n-2}$ in which Player 2 is again second. If Player 1's first move is on the clasp: when Player 1 wants the unknot, Player 2 finishes the clasp so it stays clasped, then pairs every left move with an opposite adjacent move so the board unwinds to $T_2$; when Player 1 wants a nontrivial knot, Player 2 finishes the clasp so that it can be undone by R2, after which everything left gives the trivial knot.

**$n$ odd: the unknotter wins.** If Player 1 is the unknotter, the odd number of crossings lets Player 1 force Player 2 to be the first to play on the clasp; Player 1 then finishes it and gets the unknot. If Player 1 is the knotter, Player 2 uses the even-case strategy: answer left moves with opposite adjacent moves to reduce to $T_{n-2}$ (down to $T_1$, where the unknotter wins by Question 1.6), and answer a clasp move by finishing the clasp to force the unknot. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-01.title: Counterexample
bmt-2025-power-2-01.body: It is not an invariant. An R1 move twists a strand, creating (or removing) one crossing. Starting from a circle with no crossings, one R1 move produces a diagram of the same knot (the unknot) with one crossing. (Likewise R2 changes the count by two.) $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-02.title: Trivial coloring
bmt-2025-power-2-02.body: Color every strand with the same single color. At every crossing all three strands then have the same color, so the condition holds. Hence without the 'at least two colors' requirement every diagram would be tricolorable (so the condition is what makes tricolorability interesting). $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-03.title: Coloring
bmt-2025-power-2-03.body: Trace the diagram, break it into strands at the undercrossings, and label the strands $1,2,3$ so that at each crossing the over-strand and the two under-strand ends are either three distinct labels or all equal, using at least two labels. (The official solution exhibits such a labelling in a figure; the diagram is a standard tricolorable diagram, e.g. a diagram of the figure-eight/stevedore type with a valid coloring.) A check at every crossing completes the demonstration. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-04a.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-2-04a.body:
Equivalently (checking the cases), a coloring by $0,1,2$ is valid exactly when at each crossing, with over-strand color $o$ and the two under-strand ends colored $u$ and $w$, we have $o+u+w\equiv0\pmod 3$, i.e. $w\equiv2o-u\pmod3$: indeed three equal colors or three distinct colors are exactly the triples with sum $\equiv0\pmod3$. An R1 move adds a kink on a strand $s$. After the move, $s$ is cut at the new crossing into two strands $A$ and $B$: the strand $A$ runs through the over-pass, around the loop, and ends at the under-pass, and $B$ begins just after the under-pass. At the new crossing the over-strand is $A$ and the two under-ends are $A$ and $B$, so the crossing condition says $A$, $A$, $B$ are all equal or all different; the latter is impossible, so $B$ has the same color as $A$.

Hence a coloring of the old diagram (giving $s$ one color) extends to a coloring of the new diagram by giving $A$ and $B$ that color; and conversely a coloring of the new diagram has $A$ and $B$ equal, so it gives a coloring of the old diagram with the same set of colors. So tricolorability is preserved. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-04b.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-2-04b.body:
Equivalently (checking the cases), a coloring by $0,1,2$ is valid exactly when at each crossing, with over-strand color $o$ and the two under-strand ends colored $u$ and $w$, we have $o+u+w\equiv0\pmod 3$, i.e. $w\equiv2o-u\pmod3$: indeed three equal colors or three distinct colors are exactly the triples with sum $\equiv0\pmod3$. Suppose the R2 move slides a strand $s$ (color $o$, over at both new crossings) over a strand $t$, which is cut by the two new undercrossings into $t_1$ (before), $t_2$ (between) and $t_3$ (after), with colors $x,y,z$. The crossing conditions give $y\equiv2o-x$ and $z\equiv2o-y\equiv x\pmod 3$. So $t_1$ and $t_3$ have the same color (just as the single strand $t$ had before the move), and $y$ is determined by $o$ and $x$.

Thus a coloring of the old diagram extends to the new diagram by coloring $t_2$ with $2o-x$; conversely, a coloring of the new diagram gives $t_1,t_3$ equal colors, hence a coloring of the old diagram. (If $s$ is under at both crossings, exchange the roles.) The condition "at least two colors" is also preserved: the only new color is $2o-x$, which equals $x$ when $o=x$ and otherwise is the third color, while $o$ and $x$ both already appear on $s$ and $t_1$. So tricolorability is preserved. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-04c.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-2-04c.body:
Equivalently (checking the cases), a coloring by $0,1,2$ is valid exactly when at each crossing, with over-strand color $o$ and the two under-strand ends colored $u$ and $w$, we have $o+u+w\equiv0\pmod 3$, i.e. $w\equiv2o-u\pmod3$: indeed three equal colors or three distinct colors are exactly the triples with sum $\equiv0\pmod3$. An R3 move involves three strands: $T$ (over both others), $M$ (under $T$, over $B$) and $B$ (under both). Let $t,m,b$ be the colors with which they enter the picture. At a crossing with over color $o$ the under-strand color $u$ changes to $2o-u$.

- $T$ is over at both its crossings, so it leaves with color $t$.
- $M$ passes under $T$ only, so it leaves with $2t-m$.
- $B$ passes under $T$ and $M$. In one picture $B$ meets $M$ before $M$ passes under $T$ (so $M$ has color $m$): $b\mapsto2m-b\mapsto2t-(2m-b)=2t-2m+b$. In the other picture $B$ meets $M$ after $M$ passed under $T$ (so $M$ has color $2t-m$) and $B$ passes $T$ first: $b\mapsto2t-b\mapsto2(2t-m)-(2t-b)=2t-2m+b$. The two results agree.

So the outgoing colors $(t,\,2t-m,\,2t-2m+b)$ are the same in both pictures: a coloring before the move gives a coloring after the move and vice versa, with all other strands unchanged. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-05.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-2-05.body:
The standard trefoil diagram has three crossings and three strands; give the three strands three different colors. At each crossing all three strands meeting there have different colors, so the coloring is valid and uses all three colors. Hence the trefoil is tricolorable.

The zero-crossing diagram of the unknot has a single strand, so it can use only one color; since at least two colors are required, it is not tricolorable.

Since tricolorability is unchanged by Reidemeister moves, the trefoil cannot be transformed into the unknot. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-06.title: Answer
bmt-2025-power-2-06.body:
The unknot: composing with a circle just replaces a small arc of $K$ by a path that goes around a crossing-free loop, which is $K$ again (the new diagram is related to $K$ by planar isotopy).

**Answer: the unknot**

bmt-2025-power-2-07.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-2-07.body: Pick a tricoloring of each diagram. The arcs we cut open lie on strands of each diagram; permuting the three colors (any permutation of colors preserves the crossing rule) we may assume the two cut strands have the same color. Then joining them produces strands whose colors are consistent, and every crossing of $J$ and of $K$ is unchanged, so the rule holds at every crossing of $J\#K$. At least two colors are used because one of the original colorings already used two. So $J\#K$ is tricolorable. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-08.title: Use tricolorability
bmt-2025-power-2-08.body:
Diagrams (1) and (2) are equivalent: (2) has two removable loops on the right, which disappear with R2 and R1 moves. Diagram (1) has $4$ crossings and each strand meets every other strand, so it is not tricolorable; hence (2) is not tricolorable either. Diagram (3) is tricolorable, so it cannot be equivalent to (1) and (2). Diagram (4) is equivalent to the unknot, so it is different from (1), (2), (3). By elimination, (1), (2), (5) are the same knot, and the two exceptions are (3) and (4).

**Answer: (3) and (4)**

bmt-2025-power-2-09.title: Claim and proof
bmt-2025-power-2-09.body:
**Claim.** Reversing the orientation of the knot does not change the writhe.

**Proof.** Reversing the orientation reverses the direction of both strands at every crossing. The sign of a crossing depends on whether the under-strand points to the right or left of the over-strand's direction; if both directions are reversed, the whole configuration is rotated by $180^\circ$ (in terms of the two direction vectors), so the under-strand is still on the same side relative to the over-strand's direction. Hence every crossing sign is unchanged, and so is the writhe. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-2-10a.title: Reading the diagram
bmt-2025-power-2-10a.body:
Go around the diagram in the marked direction, and for each crossing decide whether the under-strand points to the right (sign $+1$) or to the left (sign $-1$) of the over-strand's direction. Adding the signs gives the writhe of diagram (a), which is $7$ (the official answer).

**Answer: 7**

bmt-2025-power-2-10b.title: Reading the diagram
bmt-2025-power-2-10b.body:
Go around the diagram in the marked direction, and for each crossing decide whether the under-strand points to the right (sign $+1$) or to the left (sign $-1$) of the over-strand's direction. Adding the signs gives the writhe of diagram (b), which is $-7$ (the official answer).

**Answer: -7**

bmt-2025-power-2-10c.title: Reading the diagram
bmt-2025-power-2-10c.body:
Go around the diagram in the marked direction, and for each crossing decide whether the under-strand points to the right (sign $+1$) or to the left (sign $-1$) of the over-strand's direction. Adding the signs gives the writhe of diagram (c), which is $-3$ (the official answer).

**Answer: -3**

bmt-2025-power-2-10d.title: Reading the diagram
bmt-2025-power-2-10d.body:
Go around the diagram in the marked direction, and for each crossing decide whether the under-strand points to the right (sign $+1$) or to the left (sign $-1$) of the over-strand's direction. Adding the signs gives the writhe of diagram (d), which is $1$ (the official answer).

**Answer: 1**

bmt-2025-power-2-11.title: Move by move
bmt-2025-power-2-11.body:
- **R1:** adds or removes one crossing, which has sign $+1$ or $-1$, so the writhe changes by $\pm1$. Not invariant.
- **R2:** creates or deletes two crossings between the same two strands; they have opposite signs (the over-strand is the same, and the under-strand passes it from one side to the other, so the under-strand direction relative to the over-strand is to the right at one crossing and to the left at the other). The two signs cancel; the writhe is unchanged.
- **R3:** the three crossings keep their signs (the same strands cross in the same directions with the same strand on top). Writhe is unchanged.

Because R1 changes the writhe, writhe is **not** a knot invariant. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-3-01.title: Example
bmt-2025-power-3-01.body:
Take the integer tangle $[5]$: five crossings placed in a horizontal row, alternating in type, all inside the disk with the four endpoints at the corners. Any five-crossing diagram inside a disk with these four endpoints (even with a closed component) is a valid answer.

**Answer: e.g. $[5]$**

bmt-2025-power-3-02a.title: Construction
bmt-2025-power-3-02a.body:
By definition, $T_1+T_2$ is obtained as follows: place $T_1$ and $T_2$ side by side, joining the top-right endpoint of $T_1$ to the top-left endpoint of $T_2$ and the bottom-right endpoint of $T_1$ to the bottom-left endpoint of $T_2$. (Drawn on the tangles of the figure, this gives the required diagram.)

**Answer: construction as described**

bmt-2025-power-3-02b.title: Construction
bmt-2025-power-3-02b.body:
By definition, $T_1*T_2$ is obtained as follows: stack $T_1$ above $T_2$, joining the bottom endpoints of $T_1$ to the corresponding top endpoints of $T_2$. (Drawn on the tangles of the figure, this gives the required diagram.)

**Answer: construction as described**

bmt-2025-power-3-02c.title: Construction
bmt-2025-power-3-02c.body:
By definition, $-T_1$ is obtained as follows: switch every crossing of $T_1$ (over becomes under and vice versa), keeping the shape. (Drawn on the tangles of the figure, this gives the required diagram.)

**Answer: construction as described**

bmt-2025-power-3-02d.title: Construction
bmt-2025-power-3-02d.body:
By definition, $\frac1{T_2}$ is obtained as follows: rotate $T_2$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise and then switch every crossing. (Drawn on the tangles of the figure, this gives the required diagram.)

**Answer: construction as described**

bmt-2025-power-3-03a.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-3-03a.body:
If $m=0$ or $n=0$ the claim is trivial. If $m,n>0$, $[m]+[n]$ is $m$ alternating horizontal crossings followed by $n$ more of the same alternating pattern, which is exactly $m+n$ alternating horizontal crossings, $[m+n]$.

If $m$ and $n$ have opposite signs, the two tangles consist of crossings of opposite type, and the junction creates $\min(|m|,|n|)$ adjacent pairs of opposite crossings, each cancelled by an R2 move. What remains is $|m+n|$ crossings of the sign of the larger one, i.e. $[m+n]$ (the first $|m|-|n|$ crossings if $|m|>|n|$, the last $|n|-|m|$ if $|n|>|m|$); if $m=-n$ everything cancels and we get $[0]=[m+n]$.

If $m,n<0$, apply the positive case to the diagram with every crossing switched. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-3-03b.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-3-03b.body: $\frac1{[m]}*\frac1{[n]}$ is the diagram of $[-m]+[-n]$ rotated by $90^\circ$ clockwise (stacking the two rotated pieces vertically is the rotation of placing them side by side). Likewise $\frac1{[m]+[n]}$ is the diagram of $[-(m+n)]$ rotated by $90^\circ$ clockwise. By part (a), $[-m]+[-n]\sim[-(m+n)]$, and applying the same rotation to both gives the claim. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-3-04.title: Construction
bmt-2025-power-3-04.body:
Build from the inside out. (1) Take the single crossing $[-1]$ and stack it above $\frac1{[4]}$, four vertical twists, giving the tangle $[-1]*\frac1{[4]}$. (2) Add one horizontal crossing $[1]$ to its right. (3) Stack the result above $\frac1{[2]}$ (two vertical twists). The final picture is a block with one crossing over four vertical twists and a crossing to its right, with two vertical twists attached underneath.

**Answer: construction as described**

bmt-2025-power-3-05.title: Reading the picture from the inside out
bmt-2025-power-3-05.body:
The innermost piece is $[-2]$ stacked above two vertical twists, $[-2]*\frac1{[2]}$. Three horizontal crossings are added on its right, $+[3]$. One vertical crossing is stacked below this, $*\frac1{[1]}$. Finally four crossings of the negative type are added on the right, $+[-4]$. Assembling:
$$\left(\left(\left([-2]*\frac1{[2]}\right)+[3]\right)*\frac1{[1]}\right)+[-4].$$

bmt-2025-power-3-06.title: Induction
bmt-2025-power-3-06.body:
By the previous part, every rational tangle is built from the basic tangles $[0]$, $[\infty]$, $[1]$, $[-1]$, $\frac1{[1]}$, $\frac1{[-1]}$ by repeatedly adding $[\pm1]$ on the left or right and multiplying by $\frac1{[\pm1]}$ on the top or bottom.

**Base cases.** Each basic tangle is equivalent to its flips: a single crossing flipped about either axis becomes the same crossing again (the upper crossing becomes the lower one and the strands are mirrored, restoring the original crossing); $[0]$ and $[\infty]$ have no crossings.

**Step.** Suppose $T$ satisfies $T\sim T^h\sim T^v$. Then $(T+[\pm1])^h\sim T^h+[\pm1]^h\sim T+[\pm1]$, and $(T+[\pm1])^v\sim[\pm1]^v+T^v\sim[\pm1]+T\sim T+[\pm1]$ (a twist on the left can be moved to the right by flipping $T$ and using $T\sim T^h$). For products with $\frac1{[\pm1]}$ the same arguments hold with the diagram turned a quarter turn: $\left(T*\frac1{[\pm1]}\right)^v\sim T^v*\left(\frac1{[\pm1]}\right)^v\sim T*\frac1{[\pm1]}$, and the $h$-flip is handled as the $v$-flip of the sum case. By induction $P\sim P^h$ and $P\sim P^v$ for every rational tangle. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-3-07.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-3-07.body:
Rotating the diagram of $X+Y$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise puts $X$ on top of $Y$ (each rotated), and negating both gives $\frac1{X+Y}=\frac1X*\frac1Y$ (with $X$ on top). Apply this with $X=[a]$ and $Y=\frac1P$, and use $\frac1{1/P}\sim P$ (double inverse): $$\frac1{[a]+\frac1P}\sim\frac1{[a]}*P,\qquad \frac1{\frac1P+[a]}\sim P*\frac1{[a]}.$$
It remains to see $P*\frac1{[a]}\sim\frac1{[a]}*P$: rotating the whole stacked diagram by $180^\circ$ (a vertical flip followed by a horizontal flip) swaps the two factors and flips each of them, and by Question 3.6 each flip leaves $P$ and $\frac1{[a]}$ equivalent to itself (this is also the Theorem). Hence both claimed equivalences hold. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-3-08.title: Algorithm
bmt-2025-power-3-08.body:
Look at the outermost (last-applied) operation of the construction.

1. If it is a $+[m]$ on the right, move it to the left using $P+[m]\sim[m]+P$; if there is already an integer tangle on the left, merge using $[m]+[n]\sim[m+n]$.
2. If it is a product with a reciprocal tangle $\frac1{[a]}$ (on either side, moved to the left by $P*\frac1{[a]}\sim\frac1{[a]}*P$), the construction has the form $\frac1{[a]}*X$. By the Product-to-Inverse Equivalence, $\frac1{[a]}*X\sim\frac1{\frac1X+[a]}\sim\frac1{[a]+\frac1X}$ (using the sum commutation).
3. Repeat recursively on the inner tangle $X$ (whose construction is shorter) until the remaining expression is a single integer or reciprocal tangle.

Each step reduces the number of operations, so the process terminates, and the result is a continued fraction of integer tangles. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-3-09.title: Existence and uniqueness
bmt-2025-power-3-09.body:
**Existence.** Let $x_0=\frac pq>1$, $b_0=\lfloor x_0\rfloor$ and $x_0=b_0+r_0$ with $0\le r_0<1$. If $r_0=0$ stop; otherwise put $x_1=\frac1{r_0}>1$, $b_1=\lfloor x_1\rfloor$, and continue. The remainders are rationals whose denominators strictly decrease (this is the Euclidean algorithm), so the process stops with some $r_k=0$. Every $x_i$ with $i\ge1$ exceeds $1$, so the last term $b_k=x_k$ is at least $2$. Setting $a_1=b_k,\dots,a_n=b_0$ gives a valid expansion with $a_1>1$.

**Uniqueness.** In any such expansion every reciprocal term $\cfrac1{a_{n-1}+\cdots}$ lies strictly between $0$ and $1$ (all $a_i\ge1$), so $a_n$ is forced to be the integer part of $\frac pq$; subtracting it and taking the reciprocal gives the next number, to which the same argument applies. The expansion must stop exactly when the remaining value is an integer, since an extra reciprocal term would leave a nonzero fractional part. Hence the sequence is unique. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-3-10.title: Reduction and diagram moves
bmt-2025-power-3-10.body:
Since $P-\frac1Q=P+\left(-\frac1Q\right)=P+\frac1{[-Q]}$ (negation commutes with inversion), it suffices to show $$-\frac1Q\ \sim\ [-1]+\cfrac1{[1]+\cfrac1{Q-[1]}}.$$
By the Product-to-Inverse Equivalence, $\frac1{[1]+\frac1{Q-[1]}}\sim(Q-[1])*\frac1{[1]}=(Q+[-1])*\frac1{[1]}$. So the claim becomes $$-\frac1Q\sim[-1]+\big((Q+[-1])*\tfrac1{[1]}\big).$$
Diagrammatically: the right side is the tangle formed by $Q$ with one crossing to its right (the $[-1]$ inside the sum) stacked above a vertical crossing, with another horizontal crossing $[-1]$ added. Use $Q\sim Q^v$ (Question 3.6) to move the extra crossing from one side of $Q$ to the other, apply an R3 move to slide the strand of $Q$ across the crossing, and rotate the resulting picture by $90^\circ$: the result is $Q$ rotated by $90^\circ$ with all crossings switched, which is $-\frac1Q$. Reading the chain of equivalences backwards gives the statement. $\blacksquare$

(The official solution is a sequence of pictures: LHS $\to$ $Q$ with a crossing, using $Q^v\sim Q$, an $h$-flip, and R3 plus a rotation to reach the right-hand side.)

bmt-2025-power-3-11.title: Reduce to a canonical form
bmt-2025-power-3-11.body:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be rational tangles with associated fraction $\frac pq$, written in continued fraction form with integer (possibly negative) coefficients $b_i$ and $c_j$. Let $R$ be the canonical tangle $[a_k]+\cfrac1{[a_{k-1}]+\cdots+\cfrac1{[a_1]}}$ built from the unique positive expansion of $\frac pq$ (Question 3.9; for $\frac pq\le1$ use the expansion of the reciprocal of the fractional part, and treat $0$ and $\infty$ separately). We show $P\sim R$ (and likewise $Q\sim R$, so $P\sim Q$).

1. Negative coefficients: a negative integer in a fraction can be moved to the numerator by multiplying numerator and denominator by $-1$; for tangles this means switching all crossings of the corresponding sub-tangle (by $[−m]=-[m]$ and the compatibility of negation with inversion). After this, all coefficients are positive except possibly some minus signs of the form $a-\frac1b$ and possibly the outermost coefficient.
2. Use the tangle identity of Question 3.10, $P-\frac1Q\sim P-[1]+\cfrac1{[1]+\cfrac1{Q-[1]}}$ (the tangle version of $a-\frac1b=(a-1)+\cfrac1{1+\cfrac1{b-1}}$), starting from the innermost minus sign. Each application removes a minus sign, keeps the other coefficients positive after merging $[0]$ and adjacent integers by Question 3.3, and does not increase the length.
3. When no minus signs remain, merge a final coefficient $1$ with its neighbor to get the canonical expansion, which is unique by Question 3.9.

Each step is a tangle equivalence (by 3.10, Theorem 3.9, double inverse and 3.3), so $P\sim R$; similarly $Q\sim R$. Hence $P\sim Q$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-01.title: Answer
bmt-2025-power-4-01.body:
Changing one crossing, or two crossings, of the standard trefoil diagram gives a diagram equivalent to the unknot (the strands can be pulled apart by R2/R1 moves). Changing no crossings leaves the trefoil and changing all three gives the mirror-image trefoil, which are not the unknot. So any set of one or two of the crossings $1,2,3$ works, for example $\{1\}$.

**Answer: any one or two of the crossings, e.g. crossing 1**

bmt-2025-power-4-02.title: Answer
bmt-2025-power-4-02.body:
Only the diagram on the left is equivalent to the unknot (it can be undone with Reidemeister moves; the right-hand diagram is a nontrivial knot).

**Answer: left**

bmt-2025-power-4-03.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-03.body:
Think of the diagram as a knot in 3-space viewed from above. Orient the knot, pick a base point, and traverse the knot once. Resolve each crossing so that the strand passes *over* the first time we reach the crossing (and under the second time); this can be achieved by crossing changes.

Then, along the traversal, the height of the knot strictly decreases (we are always above what we meet later), except for one final vertical segment that closes the loop and creates no crossing. A knot that always moves downward and returns by one vertical segment has no crossings when viewed from the side (different points have different heights along the traversal), so it can be moved to a circle. Therefore this choice of crossings gives the unknot, and crossing changes can unknot any diagram. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-04.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-04.body: By Question 4.3 some set of $k$ crossing changes gives the unknot. If $k\le\frac N2$ we are done. Otherwise change the other $N-k<\frac N2$ crossings instead: the resulting diagram is the mirror image of the diagram obtained from the first set (every crossing is reversed), and the mirror image of an unknot is an unknot (reflect the sequence of moves). So $N-k<\frac N2$ crossing changes suffice. In either case at most $\frac N2$ changes are needed. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-05.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-05.body: Each RCC changes a fixed set of crossings (those on the boundary of the region). After the two RCCs, a given crossing is reversed if it was changed an odd number of times in total and unchanged if it was changed an even number of times. This count does not depend on the order of the two moves. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-06.title: Answer
bmt-2025-power-4-06.body:
Regions that are adjacent (share an edge segment) are separated by the knot, so $A$ cannot be the same region as $B$ or $D$. Region $C$, opposite to $A$, can coincide with $A$: this is exactly a reducible crossing.

**Answer: C**

bmt-2025-power-4-07.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-07.body:
Take a checkerboard coloring before the move and keep the colors of all regions that meet the boundary of the small disk where the move happens; then no other part of the diagram needs recoloring. We only need to color the new regions inside the disk.

- **R1.** Say the strand has region $X$ on one side and $Y$ on the other, and the new kink loop lies in $Y$'s side. The loop encloses a new small region $L$, adjacent (along the loop) only to $Y$; it meets $X$ only at the new crossing. Give $L$ the color opposite to $Y$ (the color of $X$). All adjacent pairs now have opposite colors.
- **R2.** Let strands $a$ and $b$ be pushed across each other; before the move the regions are $T$ (beyond $a$), $M$ (between $a$ and $b$) and $B$ (beyond $b$). $T$ and $B$ have the same color (both are opposite to $M$). After the move, $M$ is split into two pieces, each keeps the color of $M$, and a new bigon $G$ appears, adjacent to $T$ and to $B$ only. Give $G$ the color of $M$ (opposite to the common color of $T$ and $B$).
- **R3.** Before the move the central triangle has color $c$; the three regions sharing an edge with it have color $\bar c$ and the three regions touching it only at a vertex have color $c$ (alternating around the six boundary arcs of the disk). After the move the six outer regions keep their colors and cyclic order, but now the regions that touched the triangle only at a vertex (color $c$) are the ones sharing an edge with the new triangle, so color the new triangle $\bar c$.

In each case every pair of regions sharing an edge has opposite colors, so the new diagram is checkerboard colorable. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-08.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-08.body: Whether a diagram is checkerboard colorable depends only on the shadow of the diagram (the curve in the plane), not on which strand is over at each crossing. By Question 4.3 we may choose the crossings so that the diagram represents the unknot. Then, by Reidemeister's theorem, this diagram is obtained from the zero-crossing circle by a sequence of Reidemeister moves. The circle is checkerboard colorable (inside shaded, outside unshaded), and by Question 4.7 each Reidemeister move preserves colorability. Hence the diagram, and therefore the original diagram (same shadow), is checkerboard colorable. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-09.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-09.body: In a reduced diagram no crossing is reducible, so the four regions around each crossing are four different regions. In a checkerboard coloring the corners around a crossing alternate in shade, so exactly two of the four are shaded. Performing an RCC on every shaded region therefore changes each crossing exactly twice, and a crossing changed twice is back to its original state. Hence the diagram is unchanged. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-10.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-10.body: Traverse the knot along its orientation. The knot passes through $c$ exactly twice. Let $A$ be the arc travelled from the first visit to the second visit, and $B$ the complementary arc (from the second visit back to the first); both are nonempty. A splice respects orientation: it joins the end of $A$ (arriving at $c$ the second time) to the start of $A$ (leaving $c$ the first time), and the end of $B$ to the start of $B$. So $A$ and $B$ each become a closed loop, and no strand connects $A$ to $B$, so the result has exactly two components (they may still cross each other at other crossings, but crossings do not connect components). $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-11.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-11.body:
An RCC performed on all shaded regions flips a crossing exactly when an odd number of the distinct regions around it are shaded.

Suppose component $A$ is checkerboard colored in step 2 and $B$ is ignored. The four regions around $c$ are two regions that merge into $R$, one region coming from $A$ and one from $B$. $R$ is unshaded. The region next to $c$ that comes only from $B$ is unshaded too (it has the same shade as $R$, since $B$ does not affect the coloring of $A$). Since $R$ is unshaded and the coloring alternates for $A$, the remaining region (from $A$) is shaded. So exactly one region around $c$ is shaded and $c$ is flipped.

Now take any other crossing $d$ (not reducible, so its four regions are distinct).

- Both strands from $A$: $A$ is checkerboard colored, so two opposite regions are shaded, two distinct regions in all: $d$ is flipped twice, i.e. unchanged.
- Both strands from $B$: the coloring of $A$ ignores $B$, so all four regions around $d$ have the same shade (all shaded or all unshaded): $4$ or $0$ shaded regions, an even number: unchanged.
- One strand from $A$, one from $B$: the two regions on the shaded side of the $A$-strand are shaded and the other two unshaded, so exactly two distinct regions are shaded: unchanged.

So only $c$ is flipped. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-12.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-12.body:
Apply the three-step operation to $d$: the only crossing flipped (apart from possibly other crossings that are not reducible, which are unchanged) is $d$, since every crossing other than $d$ is not reducible. In particular if $c=d$ we are done.

If $c\ne d$, apply the three-step operation to $c$. By Question 4.11's argument, $c$ is flipped and every crossing other than $d$ is unchanged (they are not reducible). The crossing $d$ may or may not have been flipped. If $d$ was flipped, apply the three-step operation to $d$, which flips only $d$ (and nothing else). The net result is that only $c$ is changed. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-13.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-13.body:
Label the four regions around the crossing $A,B,C,D$ in order, so that the splice merges $A$ and $C$ into one region $R$ (and $B$, $D$ end up on opposite sides). A reducible crossing has two opposite corners that belong to the same region: either $\{A,C\}$ or $\{B,D\}$. It cannot be $\{B,D\}$: a path from $B$ to $D$ not meeting the knot, closed up through the crossing, would be a closed curve meeting each component of the spliced diagram exactly once, which is impossible for closed curves (a closed curve meets a closed curve an even number of times). So $A$ and $C$ are the same region.

Then from a point in $A$ we can draw a path to a point in $C$ without meeting the knot, and after the splice close it through $R$ to get a closed curve missing the spliced diagram. This curve separates $B$ from $D$: the component next to $B$ lies inside the curve and the component next to $D$ outside. Hence the two components have no common points, in particular no crossings between them. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-14.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-14.body:
Start at some reducible crossing $d\ne c$ and splice it. By Question 4.13 the two resulting components do not meet each other, so the other $k$ reducible crossings are divided between them. Say $c$ lies on component $A$, which has $a$ reducible crossings, and the other component $B$ has $b=k-a$.

If $a=k$ then $B$ is reduced and we are done. If $a<k$ then $b\ge1$, so $B$ has a reducible crossing $d'$; splice the original diagram at $d'$ instead. The component containing $c$ now contains all of $A$ (with its $a$ reducible crossings) and also the crossing $d$, which is reducible, so it has at least $a+1$ reducible crossings. The number of reducible crossings on the component containing $c$ strictly increases and is at most $k$, so repeating the step we eventually reach a splice where the component containing $c$ has exactly $k$ reducible crossings and the other component is reduced. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2025-power-4-15.title: Proof
bmt-2025-power-4-15.body:
By Question 4.14 we can splice $D$ at a reducible crossing $d$ into a component $A$ containing $c$ and $k$ reducible crossings and a reduced component $B$. By the inductive hypothesis, applied to the diagram $A$, there is a set of shaded regions (coming from a series of RCCs) that flips $c$ and no other crossing of $A$. We now check the crossings of $B$ and the crossing $d$ in $D$.

The relevant regions are $X$, the region of $A$ that bordered $d$ before the splice, and $Y$, the region surrounding $B$ in $A$ (together with all interior regions of $B$, since the strands of $B$ are ignored when finding regions for $A$). $Y$ is either completely shaded or completely unshaded, including the interior of the box containing $B$, so each crossing inside $B$ is surrounded by $0$ or $4$ shaded regions (an even number) and is not flipped. If we later recolor $B$ (cases 3 and 4 below), each crossing of $B$ is surrounded by exactly two distinct shaded regions, since $B$ is reduced, so it is still not flipped.

It remains to make sure $d$ is not flipped. The four regions around $d$ are $X$, $Y$ (above and below $d$, the same region) and the region opposite $X$ (to the right of $d$, bordering $B$).

1. $X$ and $Y$ unshaded: no shaded region at $d$; $d$ is not flipped; nothing to do.
2. $X$ unshaded, $Y$ shaded: $d$ appears to have three shaded corners, but two of them are the same region $Y$, so there are exactly $2$ distinct shaded regions: not flipped; nothing to do.
3. $X$ shaded, $Y$ unshaded: only one shaded region at $d$, so $d$ would flip. Fix this by shading the region opposite $X$ and checkerboard coloring $B$ accordingly. Crossings of $B$ remain unflipped (they touch two distinct shaded regions), crossings of $A$ are unchanged because the region outside $B$ keeps its shading, and now $d$ has $2$ distinct shaded regions.
4. $X$ and $Y$ shaded: $d$ has $3$ distinct shaded regions; unshade the region opposite $X$ and recolor $B$ accordingly, so that $d$ has $2$ distinct shaded regions, with the other crossings as in case 3.

In every case we obtain a set of shaded regions whose RCCs change $c$ and no other crossing. $\blacksquare$

By induction, in any knot diagram any single crossing can be changed by RCC moves alone, so RCCs are an unknotting operation.
